summary.title: We gave AI agents a mobile dev environment
summary.idea: Mobile agents were limited by laptop resources and Linux lacking iOS tooling, so Shopify gave each agent session a remote, pre-warmed Mac with an emulator and a skill that teaches it to prove its work.
howItWorks: Keep a pool of warm Macs with main checked out, tools installed and apps built, cutting setup from 30+ minutes to minutes.
Each agent claims a Mac over SSH, syncs its branch, and attaches a prebuilt Android VM for testing.
A CLI wraps the fiddly SSH flags, and tmux panes let the agent watch long-running tasks instead of sleeping.
A skill tells the agent to reproduce a bug, record it, fix it, then record the same steps again for before and after.
A cheap classifier tags every mobile conversation by outcome, and failures feed an LLM that improves the skill.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent says it can't verify something, write a skill plus a small CLI wrapper that gives it a remote environment and requires before-and-after screenshots or recordings with every fix.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building remote environments for agents that must build and test real apps, or want a concrete loop for improving agent skills from failed sessions.
summary.quote: So we created a skill to teach agents how to test their changes and prove their work.

verdict.reason: Shopify walks through its working mobile agent harness, and the page supports every card claim: a warm Mac pool, a CLI wrapping SSH, tmux panes the agent watches instead of sleeping, before-and-after recordings as proof, and failed sessions classified to improve the skill; it loses points because there is no code and the infrastructure is heavy for most teams to copy.

summary.title: Context Engineering Starts with Retrieval
summary.idea: Agents burn their limited context on clumsy searches, oversized results and stale or irrelevant text; the fix is cheap search first, results saved to files, and subagents doing the reading.
howItWorks: Search before reading: glob matches file names, grep finds matching lines, and read_file pages through 100 lines at a time.
Oversized tool results (over about 20,000 tokens) are saved to a file; the agent gets the path plus a short preview.
A custom retrieval tool writes each hit to a file and returns only the paths, not the full text.
A chunk-analyst subagent reads one retrieved file each, in parallel, and returns key facts with the source URL.
Filter by date or use a search API for freshness, and check that answers cite the expected sources.
summary.stealThis: Next time you build a RAG or search tool for an agent, make it save each result to a file and return only the paths, then hand each path to a subagent that summarises it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a research-style agent whose context fills up with search results, and want working code for the retrieve, offload, delegate pattern.
summary.quote: Return pointers instead of payloads.

verdict.reason: Teaches a transferable 'retrieve, offload, delegate' pattern with working code: a retrieval tool writes hits to files and returns only paths, and per-file subagents return key facts with sources; it docks for being framed around LangChain's Deep Agents harness, though the pattern ports to any harness.

summary.title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary.idea: Shared team agents need more than a prompt: LangChain's internal agents for sales, engineering and marketing all rely on the same five building blocks, including per-person identity and scoped memory.
howItWorks: Put the agent in the team's chat tool, with its own app, so people can DM or tag it.
Split identity: act as the invoking user for personal tools, and use fixed credentials for shared services.
Limit risky tools by context, such as email only in DMs and posting rights for whitelisted users.
Keep two memory tiers, global and per-user, and let the agent choose where each fact goes.
Run code in a sandbox with a secret proxy, and trigger many runs by schedule or event.
summary.stealThis: Before you give a team agent access to real services, list each tool and mark it as acting as the user or as the agent, then hide the user-identity tools in shared channels.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're rolling out one agent to a whole team and need to decide identity, memory and scheduling, and can tolerate a LangChain-flavored tooling pitch.
summary.quote: It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others

verdict.reason: The page teaches transferable patterns for multiplayer agents, such as splitting tools into on-behalf-of-user versus fixed-credential identity, hiding user-identity tools outside DMs, whitelisting risky operations and two-tier memory, though it offers no code or before/after evidence and ends in a Managed Deep Agents pitch.

summary.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here's Why.
summary.idea: Models solve hard problems when a harness lets them run many cheap depth-first attempts, prunes them with a verifier, and feeds every failure back as a negative hint.
howItWorks: A drafter writes solver prompts from model priors plus a running list of failed approaches, which act as negative hints.
A solver runs one or many candidate attempts, using parallel subagents to pursue different paths to completion.
A verifier checks finished arguments automatically, so spending compute on uncertain ideas becomes rational.
Prompts add standing adversarial checks for known failure modes, plus a line telling the model not to quit when approaches fail.
Predict where this works: problems with few key insights and a small branching factor at each step.
summary.stealThis: Next time an agent task keeps failing, add a drafter step that rewrites the prompt each round with a list of what already failed and why, plus standing checks for those failure modes.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building multi-agent loops with verifiers and want a mental model for which problems are worth pointing them at.
summary.quote: Every one of these lines is a failed path, written up as an instruction.

verdict.reason: The essay is mostly analysis of why models succeed at math, but it does teach a transferable drafter/solver/verifier loop: fold each failed attempt back into the next prompt as a negative hint and promote known failure modes to standing adversarial checks, backed by the quoted CDC prompt. The setup is the author's reconstruction of what OpenAI likely did, not a demonstrated harness, so the technique is thin.

summary.title: Make coding agents prove their work
summary.idea: An agent's own summary describes what it meant to do, not what happened, so require checkable evidence in every report and enforce the fast checks with a Stop hook.
howItWorks: Run checks cheapest first: typecheck, lint, build with prerender, bundle budget, then screenshots at desktop and phone widths.
Every report must include changed files, pasted command output, test counts, budget numbers, screenshot paths, and a section on what was not checked.
A Claude Code Stop hook runs typecheck and lint; exit code 2 returns errors to the agent so it keeps working.
The hook checks the stop_hook_active flag and allows one forced retry, avoiding endless loops on unfixable errors.
A CI budget script gzips the initial JS and CSS, fails above 250 KB, and prints numbers on every build.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task, add a Stop hook that runs typecheck and lint and exits 2 on failure, and require the report to end with a 'what I did not check' section.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent changes on trust and want the full hook script, budget check and Playwright screenshot script to copy.
summary.quote: An agent's summary of its own work is the least reliable part of its output

verdict.reason: The page teaches concrete verification techniques with full code: a Claude Code Stop hook that exits 2 on typecheck or lint failure and uses a stop_hook_active guard against loops, a mandatory evidence report with a 'what I did not check' section, a gzip bundle budget in CI, and Playwright screenshots at two widths, all of which the card accurately reflects.

summary.title: An agent PR that only says 'fixed' makes the reviewer redo the diagnosis
summary.idea: Agent PRs that just say 'done, tests pass' force reviewers to re-derive the bug; a fixed PR template demanding reproduction and before/after evidence makes the claim checkable in minutes.
howItWorks: Use a PR template with blank fields: reproduction, before/after check, touched scope, uncovered assumptions, and revert and risk.
The reproduction field holds the exact failing command, the expected result and the actual result.
Name the check that failed and now passes, and say whether it was newly added or already existed.
Add 'repro command present' and 'failing check named' to the agent's done-checklist so empty fields block completion.
Before accepting 'done', ask the agent to paste the failing log line and the command that reproduced it.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-opened pull request, add a template with reproduction, before/after check, scope and assumptions fields, and have the agent refuse to mark done while any is blank.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck on reviewing agent pull requests and keep re-running failures to confirm a fix is real.
summary.quote: A green suite proves the current checks pass; it rarely proves the specific bug that broke is closed.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: an evidence-based agent PR template (repro command, before/after check, scope, assumptions, revert) wired into the done-checklist, plus a cheap 'paste the failing log line' check, but it's short and has no real example template, repo or before/after.

summary.title: Your AI Agent Says “Done.” What Did It Actually Verify?
summary.idea: Agents report 'done' with confident summaries that are not proof, so define observable acceptance criteria up front and require a completion report listing the exact checks run, results and what stayed unverified.
howItWorks: State the expected behavior as an observable outcome before the agent starts, including a regression test requirement.
Require a completion report: what changed, commands run, pass or fail results, and what could not be checked.
Confirm the new regression test fails against the original code and passes after the fix.
Scrutinize test edits such as skipped tests, removed assertions, swapped mocks, or changed expected values.
Treat blocked checks as unfinished verification and complete them elsewhere before relying on the result.
summary.stealThis: Paste the post's reusable completion-report prompt into your next agent coding task, asking for exact checks run, test changes made, and what remains unverified, then review the test diff separately before merging.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent-written code and want a checklist plus a reusable prompt for spotting weak or fake verification, with useful pitfalls in the comments.
summary.quote: A command mentioned in a summary is still a claim until you can confirm its execution.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: upfront observable acceptance criteria plus a reusable completion-report prompt (exact checks run, fail-first regression test, test-edit disclosure, unverified list), and the card accurately reflects the page, though the evidence is a small illustrative example rather than a real repo or before-and-after.

summary.title: The State of Context Engineering
summary.idea: Long-running agents get stuck on bad context, fixated ideas, and stale memory; the answer is a small set of harness moves like loadout, quarantine, pruning, offloading and periodic context resets.
howItWorks: Tool loadout: a fast small model checks each tool against the request and exposes only the relevant subset.
Quarantine: wrap a subagent as a tool so it starts with a blank history in the same environment.
Pruning and pre-compaction filtering: a small model flags old turns as still needed or not, then you summarize what remains.
Against context inertia, write a short note every ninety minutes or so and clear the conversation, keeping files and artifacts.
Treat repeated, all-caps instructions in a prompt as a sign you are fighting the model's training.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent loops on one idea or acts oddly past about 200,000 tokens, have it write a handoff note to a file, clear the context, and restart from that note.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building or tuning an agent harness and want the failure modes behind context rot, plus the short DSPy sketches showing each fix.
summary.quote: Our output is the product of the context and the weights.

verdict.reason: The talk teaches concrete harness moves the page actually describes: small-model tool loadout, subagent quarantine, per-turn pruning, filter-before-compaction, and periodic note-and-clear resets against context inertia, backed by cited papers and short DSPy sketches, though the code itself isn't shown in the text.

summary.title: Spec-Driven Development with AI Coding Agents: Specs, Tasks, Security
summary.idea: Agent output is hard to review when intent lives only in chat; writing requirements, design and task files first, with testable EARS criteria and security rules, makes review cheaper and checkable.
howItWorks: The agent drafts requirements, design and tasks files; a human approves each phase before the next begins.
Write each acceptance criterion in EARS form, so it maps to a test setup, action and assertion.
Tag criteria with versioned OWASP ASVS IDs and keep project-wide rules in AGENTS.md or a constitution.
List approved dependencies with pinned versions in the spec, and let CI fail on any unapproved direct dependency.
Define a task as done only when its linked test passes in CI, and update the spec in the same pull request.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-built feature, write each acceptance criterion as 'If [trigger], then the [system] shall [response]' with an ID, and require the agent's test names to carry those IDs.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing large agent diffs and want a full worked spec, task list and CI check to copy.
summary.quote: A ticked box in tasks.md is an assertion, not proof.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a tool-agnostic spec-first workflow with a full worked example: EARS acceptance criteria with IDs mapped to setup, action and assertion, requirement IDs in test names, an approved-dependency list, and a copyable CI job that fails on unapproved direct dependencies; the Safeguard marketing is incidental, and the card matches the page accurately.

summary.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
summary.idea: Agents that work in a demo drift after prompt, tool or model changes, so run a small eval dataset on every change and compare per-case scores against a baseline.
howItWorks: Write a small dataset of about four cases covering different behaviors, so it runs in under a minute on every change.
Generate agent traces, then grade them with an LLM-as-judge metric, and save the full result JSON, not just the mean.
Diff the baseline and candidate result files per case to see where a change helped or hurt.
Run a nightly job on a bigger regression set, with a script that exits non-zero if the mean drops past a threshold.
Keep the dataset (inputs) and eval config (expectations) in separate committed files so you know which half changed.
summary.stealThis: Before your next prompt or model swap, run the same small eval set before and after, then compare per-case scores rather than the mean to see exactly which behavior moved.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're swapping prompts or models on an agent and want a concrete eval loop with regression alerting, including worked before-and-after numbers.
summary.quote: Snapshot result files, not scores.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable eval loop with real before-and-after numbers and code: a tiny four-case dataset run on every change, saved full result JSON with per-case diffs instead of means, and a plain Python threshold script that exits non-zero for nightly alerting; it uses Google's CLI, but the pattern isn't locked to it.

summary.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
summary.idea: Having an LLM emit schema-constrained JSON for UI is slow and error-prone, so let the model write a compact intermediate format and have deterministic code compile and validate it into the real protocol.
howItWorks: The SDK generates both the prompt syntax section and the compiler from your catalog's JSON schema, so the model can't use components you lack.
You pick the format with one argument, inference_format_factory, when creating the generator; the catalog and renderers stay unchanged.
Express writes one Python-like statement per line with positional arguments, needing up to 3x fewer tokens than direct JSON.
Macros let the model write only an ID like OrderStatus("ord_42"), while your code fetches and fills in the real values.
For screens with known shapes, a decision model answers typed questions from a Markdown grammar and code builds the component tree.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent that emits structured output, have the model write a terse line-based DSL and compile it with deterministic code that validates against your schema, rather than asking for raw JSON.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents that output structured UI or other schema-bound output and need lower latency without losing validation.
summary.quote: generating JSON trees constrained by a complex JSON schema is slow and error-prone for LLMs.

verdict.reason: This is a product-release post, but it teaches a transferable pattern beyond the A2UI SDK: have the model write a terse line-based DSL, then compile and validate it with deterministic code generated from your schema, plus ID-only macros so code fills in real data; the evidence is thin, with eval results mentioned but not shown.

summary.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
summary.idea: Letting a model do pricing math and juggle every task in one prompt makes chat commerce unreliable, so this prototype splits work across specialist agents, moves state into Redis, and hands arithmetic to deterministic tools.
howItWorks: A cheap supervisor model classifies each message and routes it to a profile, inventory or transaction specialist, each with a small focused prompt.
Cart and customer state live in Redis keyed by phone number, so the model sees only the current intent and a cart summary.
Totals, tax and delivery fees come from a plain Python tool, calculate_cart_totals, never from the model's own arithmetic.
The model sees only a masked payment label, while the charge tool receives the tokenized customer ID.
Automated tests cover pricing, HMAC signature checks, the three-turn flow and charge execution.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent touches money, dates or any exact calculation, move that logic into a tested function exposed as a tool and add a unit test asserting the exact output.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a multi-agent workflow on LangGraph and want a worked example of routing, deterministic tools and externalized session state.
summary.quote: A core tenet of our blueprint is: delegate arithmetic to deterministic tools.

verdict.reason: The page teaches transferable harness patterns: deterministic tools for pricing math (calculate_cart_totals), state kept outside the model in Redis, a cheap supervisor routing to small specialist prompts, and masked payment labels, all backed by code and test output; but the core idea is familiar and the piece is heavy on GCP infrastructure, so it's thin as a teaching item.

summary.title: How We Built Our Design Agent
summary.idea: A design agent produced generic AI-looking work until the team gave it designers' principles, deterministic checks, a per-thread sandbox and async subagents, so non-designers can ship on-brand assets from Slack.
howItWorks: A router skill maps each kind of request to a specialist skill, and its description says when not to use it.
Measurable rules, like default capitalization, run as deterministic code gates; subjective calls go into skills as written reasoning.
Work moves storyboard, animatic, production; code enforces that assembly waits until every act passes review.
The main agent acts as chief of staff, starting async subagents with briefs that name file ownership and validation.
A fast loop saves feedback to capped memory files; a slow loop turns lessons from finished jobs into skill updates.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent workflow ships, split its rules in two: put anything measurable and order-critical into a code gate, and keep taste and judgment in the skill prompt.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents for non-engineering teammates, or you want a detailed look at routers, gates, async subagents and memory loops in a real harness.
summary.quote: The order that must always hold lives in code, and the judgment stays in the prompt.

verdict.reason: The page walks through a working harness and what broke along the way, and its techniques transfer beyond the vendor's product: a router skill, code gates for order-critical steps, async subagents with ownership briefs, and AGENTS.md memory capped at 200 lines. It backs this with an open-source repo, though the 'real-setups' theme fits better than 'non-engineers'.

summary.title: How to Build Proactive, Always-On Agents with the Schedules SDK in Managed Deep Agents
summary.idea: Agents that act without being prompted are mostly cron jobs: a scheduler fires a stored prompt, and the agent gets tools to create, list and delete its own schedules.
howItWorks: Run a cron server that stores a schedule, a prompt, and any skills or permissions the run needs.
Each scheduled run is just the saved prompt, using the thread and memory of the user who created it.
Define fixed schedules as files, such as a weekday 8am sales digest with a timezone.
Wrap create, list and delete calls as agent tools so users can set up recurring tasks you didn't anticipate.
Use the same cron pattern for memory consolidation, inbox triage every ten minutes, follow-up reminders, and orchestrators that wake to check on subtasks.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent project, add a nightly cron that prompts the agent to condense the day's conversations into long-term memory notes, then expose set, list and delete schedule tools.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building an agent that should act on its own, such as digests, triage or memory consolidation, and want working schedule code.
summary.quote: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable pattern: run agents as cron jobs that fire stored prompts, and expose create/list/delete schedule tools so the agent can manage its own recurring tasks. The card matches the page, but it passes only thinly because the code is tied to LangChain's Managed Deep Agents SDK and the memory-consolidation 'dreaming' idea is described without implementation.

summary.title: How to build evidence-grounded agent memory with OpenWiki and Graphs
summary.idea: Agents answering questions across many documents rebuild context from scratch and cite inconsistent evidence; a compiled wiki plus a deterministic evidence graph of typed citation edges makes answers more accurate and repeatable.
howItWorks: Compile source documents into linked wiki pages where each claim cites source lines and a hash of those lines.
When a source changes, the hash changes, so stale claims are flagged without a model call.
Split documents into uniquely identified paragraphs so claims point to exact passages, not whole documents.
Materialize citations as typed edges such as cites, refers_to and supersedes, with no extra model calls.
Give the agent two tools: locate finds a starting node, expand follows typed edges and stops at branches.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent works across a pile of policies or docs, turn its existing citations into typed edges (refers_to, supersedes) and expose simple locate and expand tools for following them.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents that reason across many linked documents and need reproducible, auditable answers, or you're weighing whether memory is worth its cost.
summary.quote: The graph’s job is evidence navigation, not modeling everything the organization knows.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable memory-and-tool pattern: hash-linked claims flag stale content, citations become typed edges, and locate/expand tools navigate them, backed by a controlled benchmark and tool signatures; the setup is fairly heavy and tied to having a cited wiki first.

summary.title: You can just ask AI to do things
summary.idea: Most people are bottlenecked on noticing which tasks an agent could take over, so the author walks through the chores he now hands to agents in his daily engineering work.
howItWorks: Ask the agent to start the dev server and run happy-path requests with curl instead of doing it by hand.
Have an agent poll metrics and logs before and after a deploy or flag flip, even hourly for the rest of the day.
Ask subagents to get second opinions on a code change from other models, then skim or let the main agent absorb the feedback.
Schedule a 6am agent job that scans unread messages, flags questions and problems, and does preliminary log research.
Let the agent set up its own skills, log access and MCP servers, and tidy its own stale sessions.
summary.stealThis: Before your next deploy or feature-flag flip, ask an agent to poll your logs and metrics before and after the change and report anything odd.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're an engineer who suspects you're doing tedious tasks by hand that an agent could handle, and want concrete examples from a daily workflow.
summary.quote: I don’t ask the agent to do everything.

verdict.reason: An engineer's actual daily harness with copyable techniques, such as having an agent poll logs and metrics before and after deploys, running curl happy paths against the dev server, getting second opinions from other models via subagents, and a scheduled 6am triage job; each is only lightly explained, with no code or before-and-after evidence.

summary.title: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
summary.idea: Coding agents normally need the cloud, so this walkthrough runs OpenCode against a local Qwen model through Ollama, locks it down, and uses existing unchanged tests as proof the offline fix works.
howItWorks: Pull the model and dependencies while online, then launch the exact setup once before disconnecting.
opencode.json points both models at local Ollama, enables only the local provider, blocks web tools, and asks before edits or shell commands.
Start from failing unittest cases so the agent has a concrete target independent of its own explanation.
Prompt the agent with the exact test command and forbid changing tests or installing anything.
After the agent exits, rerun the original tests yourself and inspect the small diff.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task, put the exact test command in the prompt, tell it not to edit tests or install anything, and rerun the untouched tests yourself afterward.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're curious about running a coding agent fully locally and want the config, Ollama commands and example exercises to reproduce it.
summary.quote: Using existing tests gives the agent a concrete target.

verdict.reason: The page gives a reproducible offline harness: OpenCode configured for local Ollama only, web tools blocked, and permission prompts before edits or shell commands. Its verification habit is sound: give the exact test command, forbid editing tests, then rerun them yourself. The card matches the page, but the demo is a one-line toy fix, so it's thin.

summary.title: harness-template
summary.idea: Agents drift without a stated goal, state, or independent checks, so this template installs a goal, one-item backlog, boot hook, guard hooks and a read-only reviewer subagent in one command.
howItWorks: A session-start hook injects the goal, current backlog item and git state so the agent always begins from real state.
The /ship skill takes one backlog item: plan, human OK, build, read-only reviewer subagent checks, then record and commit.
A Stop hook runs the project's check script and sends the agent back to work if the check is red.
A Bash guard hook refuses force-push, reset --hard and rm -rf, and asks before migrations and deploys.
The reviewer has no write tools, and non-blocking findings become bug or debt items in the backlog.
summary.stealThis: Add a Stop hook that runs your test command and blocks the agent from finishing while it fails, the next time you set up a Claude Code project.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building your own agent harness and want working hook scripts, a maker/checker split and a way to update it over time.
summary.quote: Every file here encodes an assumption about what the model can't do.

verdict.reason: The repo ships working Claude Code hook scripts that a reader can copy: a Stop hook that blocks finishing on a red check, a PreToolUse Bash guard, a session-start state injection, and a read-only reviewer subagent, and the card describes these accurately; it is held below 9 because it has zero stars and only anecdotal results (about 70 items shipped across three projects).

summary.title: feat(skills): add ui-evidence for before and after UI screenshots
summary.idea: Hand-taken UI screenshots are flaky and tie up shared dev stacks, so a skill builds isolated before and after copies of the app and captures light and dark screenshots automatically.
howItWorks: `up` builds a git ref in a detached worktree, then starts a labeled Postgres container and the API on free ports.
A scenario file seeds users and sessions through SQL and everything else through the API; RPCs missing on the old ref are reported, not faked.
`shoot` uses headless Chromium, sets the theme, waits for network idle and animations, and writes names like shot-before-dark.png.
A missing selector or an unapplied theme fails the shot, and its screenshot goes to a failed/ folder instead of the evidence.
`table` builds the PR-body table, `gh pr edit --attach` uploads the images, and `down --all` cleans up containers and worktrees.
summary.stealThis: Next time an agent changes a UI, wrap screenshot capture in a skill that forks into a subagent, fails loudly on missing selectors, and returns only paths and failures to the main session.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent-made UI changes and want a repeatable, isolated way to attach before and after proof to every PR.
summary.quote: A selector that never appears, or a theme the page did not apply, fails the shot.

verdict.reason: Concrete, evidenced proof-of-work technique: a skill that spins up isolated before/after worktree stacks, captures theme-verified screenshots with Playwright, fails loudly into a failed/ folder, forks into a subagent returning only paths and failures, and attaches images to the PR via gh. The PR includes exact commands and verification results, and the card accurately reflects the page.

summary.title: Claude Reviewing Claude: Anthropic's Code Review Process Has No Second Model
summary.idea: Reviewers that are all the same model share blind spots, so votes aren't independent; adding a review pass from a different model, verified by the host agent, catches bugs the first model keeps missing.
howItWorks: After Claude reviews a diff, run a second model (Codex, Grok or Gemini) on the same diff.
Have Claude check each second-model finding against the code and discard false ones; about 1 in 4 were wrong.
Cap review rounds at three, then stop and ask the author to rethink instead of looping.
Turn past incidents into an eval set and score reviewer prompt, tool or model changes against it.
Keep humans on risky paths like billing and CI files; an agent's approval never counts as a person's.
summary.stealThis: Before merging your next agent-written PR, run a different lab's model on the diff and have your main agent verify each finding against the code before you act on it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're relying on one model to write and review agent code and want evidence, log numbers and concrete bugs a second reviewer caught.
summary.quote: Run the same model again and you get the same miss.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete cross-model review layer: a second lab's model reviews the diff and the host agent verifies findings, about 1 in 4 of which were wrong, with round caps and incident-based reviewer evals, backed by personal log numbers and specific caught bugs, though the evidence is admittedly rough and has no code or repo.

summary.title: How to automate weekly reports with AI agents (and keep the numbers honest)
summary.idea: Agent-written reports can state wrong numbers fluently, so split the job: read-only pulls save raw data, code computes every figure, and the agent writes only the interpretation.
howItWorks: Give the agent read-only credentials per source, such as a restricted Stripe key, so a scheduled job cannot change anything.
One script per source saves the raw response with its date window and row totals on every run.
Week-over-week changes and totals are computed by code from saved files, so the model never does arithmetic.
Each metric is a value, 'not measured' or 'blocked', never a silent zero when a call fails.
Each source gets a declared data lag, and the window ends before it, so half-empty days are not read as drops.
summary.stealThis: Before your next recurring report, move every number into a script that reads saved raw pulls, and instruct the writing step to label failed metrics 'not measured' and to say 'cause not established' for unexplained swings.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're handing recurring reporting to an agent and want to see a real run that caught a misleading impressions spike and a failed API call.
summary.quote: The weekly report shouldn't need your approval to exist. It should need your approval to be sent.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable reporting harness that matches the card: read-only per-source pulls saved with row totals, numbers computed in code, declared data lags, 'not measured' instead of silent zeros, and writing rules like 'cause not established', backed by a real run that caught a spike and a failed API call; it loses points for having no code and for coming from a vendor.

summary.title: agent-harness-template
summary.idea: Agents start each session blind, claim "done" without running anything, and review their own code. This template swaps longer prompts for rule files, a single check command, stop hooks and a fresh-context reviewer.
howItWorks: One AGENTS.md holds hard rules with reasons, a code map and commands, and every tool reads it.
A stop hook runs quick checks on changed files, and the agent can't finish until make check passes.
PROGRESS.md and docs/decisions.md carry state between sessions; a handoff skill updates them and a start hook displays them.
A reviewer subagent reads only the diff in a fresh context against REVIEW.md, for at most two rounds.
A fill prompt mines past agent sessions, turning repeated corrections into rules and checks.
summary.stealThis: Next time an agent repeats a mistake twice, add a failing check to your single check script instead of another paragraph in the instructions file.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're setting up a repo for Claude Code or Codex and want a working set of hooks, skills and review files to copy.
summary.quote: A mistake that happened twice becomes a check in scripts/check.sh, not another paragraph.

verdict.reason: A copyable MIT repo that turns the harness into files and checks: AGENTS.md rules with reasons, a single make check behind a stop hook, a PROGRESS.md handoff, a fresh-context diff reviewer and turning repeated mistakes into checks, all of which the card reports accurately, though it has zero stars and no before/after evidence.

summary.title: My New Agentic Workflow
summary.idea: Running many parallel agents left the author unable to track them, so he now optimizes for minimizing human attention and picks one of three workflows per task based on how much attention it needs.
howItWorks: Rate each work item by impact and by how much human attention it needs, instead of by build cost.
High impact, high attention: one Claude Code session, fanning work out to subagents that each open PRs.
Most other work goes through a 'factory' that puts the delivery lifecycle on rails, with optional check-ins at planning and code review.
The factory automates PR polling, CI fixes, unblocking agents and bug fixes, and he can approve plans or merge automatically.
Low-priority one-shots use a /goal loop or custom harness, such as rustify, which walks the import graph and fails CI if the port lags.
summary.stealThis: Before your next batch of agent work, label each task by how much of your attention it needs, then route it to a single supervised session, an automated pipeline, or a one-shot loop.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running several agents in parallel, losing track of what each is doing, and want a way to decide where your review attention goes.
summary.quote: Instead of optimizing for maximizing agent productivity, I changed the optimization function to be minimizing human attention.

verdict.reason: The card accurately reflects the author's real setup: triaging tasks on an impact/human-attention matrix and routing each to supervised subagents, an automated delivery 'factory', or a one-shot harness like rustify. It passes but stays thin, because the factory's mechanics are never shown and the evidence is only PR counts.

summary.title: docs(agents): require a pr-skill body and before/after screenshots for UI changes
summary.idea: Reviewers can't judge UI changes from diffs or after-only screenshots, so the repo's AGENTS.md now requires a skill-written PR body and a before/after screenshot pair as evidence.
howItWorks: AGENTS.md rule: write the PR body with the pr skill, giving Summary, Evidence and Merge Danger sections.
Any diff that changes what a user sees must embed a before/after screenshot pair in Evidence.
Images live on a pr-assets/<pr-number>-<slug> branch, so they stay out of the diff and are linked by raw URL.
A review agent checks the PR against the constitution and reports findings with path:line and a concrete failure each.
Long delivery guidance moved out of AGENTS.md into reference docs, keeping the always-loaded file short.
summary.stealThis: Add a rule to your agent instructions that any UI-changing PR must include a before/after screenshot pair, and try it on your next agent-authored front-end change.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're writing an AGENTS.md for a team and want to see a real review agent catch broken pointers and sequencing flaws in it.
summary.quote: An after-only screenshot does not prove the change; the reviewer needs the pair.

verdict.reason: The PR shows a copyable AGENTS.md rule requiring before/after screenshot pairs, hosted on a separate pr-assets branch, plus a review agent that reports path:line findings, though the merged rule has an unresolved PR-number sequencing flaw and no worked UI example.

summary.title: stackdiff: Review big agent changes locally, as a stack of small chunks
summary.idea: Large agent diffs are hard to review in one go, so stackdiff has the agent split its change into ordered chunks with an overview, and you review them one at a time locally.
howItWorks: The agent lists hunks with `stackdiff hunks`, then writes a plan that groups them into ordered chunks plus an overview.
`stackdiff plan` checks and saves the plan, then `stackdiff open` shows the chunks in a local browser UI.
You comment on lines, approve each chunk, or chat with the agent to reorder or merge chunks.
`stackdiff wait` blocks the agent until you submit a review, then it replies to or resolves each thread.
If the agent edits an approved chunk, the approval clears and you see only what changed since your last review.
summary.stealThis: Before your next large agent change, ask the agent to split its diff into an ordered plan of small chunks with a short overview, and review it chunk by chunk, approving each one.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck on reviewing big agent diffs and want a local, chunked review loop that feeds comments back to the agent.
summary.quote: Review big agent changes locally, as a stack of small chunks.

verdict.reason: The page backs every claim on the card: an open-source, agent-agnostic skill and CLI where the agent groups diff hunks into an ordered chunk plan with an overview, and `stackdiff wait` blocks it until a chunk-by-chunk review comes back. Approvals clear when a chunk changes, and the reviewer then sees only what changed since their last review, so the technique transfers even without the tool, though the brand-new repo has no evidence of real-world use.

summary.title: coletebou/dx: Dotfiles for running fleets of coding agents
summary.idea: Running many coding agents at once gets messy: context fills, sessions die, and memory is lost. This dotfiles repo packages hooks, handoff chains, worktrees and memory sweeps so one person's fleet stays manageable.
howItWorks: A context-advisor hook suggests starting a fresh session before the context window fills up.
cc-handoff moves a long session into a new one through a written brief.
parallel-worktrees runs N Claude Code or Codex sessions in separate git worktrees and tmux windows with a merged log.
A background reflector files what each session learned and left open; a nightly sweep consolidates memory.
The adversarial-review skill requires every finding to survive refuters before it counts.
summary.stealThis: Before your next long agent session fills its context, have the agent write a handoff brief (done, open, next steps) and start a fresh session from that brief instead of pushing on.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running several coding agents in parallel and want working hooks, handoff and memory scripts to adapt rather than build from scratch.
summary.quote: Everything is opt-in. Take one plugin, one component, or all of it.

verdict.reason: This is one person's working harness for Claude Code and Codex, with real code to copy: a context-advisor hook, cc-handoff session handoff through a written brief, parallel worktrees, a session reflector with a nightly memory sweep, and adversarial review. The card matches the README, though the README describes these tools more than it explains how they work, and the brief's 'done, open, next steps' structure is the card's own gloss.

summary.title: Give Claude Code a read-only reviewer subagent in one file
summary.idea: The agent that wrote code judges it poorly, so a separate reviewer subagent with only read tools and its own context can check the diff without being able to change anything.
howItWorks: Save a markdown file at .claude/agents/reviewer.md with a name, a description and a prompt.
Restrict its tools to Read, Grep, Glob and Bash(git diff:*) so it cannot edit files.
The prompt tells it to read changed files in full and list only real problems with file, line and fix.
It runs in its own context, so long reviews don't consume the main session's memory.
Call it by asking, or add a CLAUDE.md line to run it before every commit.
summary.stealThis: Before your next commit, create a reviewer subagent with read-only tools, and have it use git diff HEAD plus git status --short so staged and new files are included.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck on reviewing agent output and want a cheap first-pass reviewer, plus the comment-thread fixes for its blind spots.
summary.quote: The agent that wrote the code is a poor judge of it.

verdict.reason: The page gives a copyable read-only reviewer subagent file with a restricted tool list and a CLAUDE.md pre-commit trigger, and a comment tested and fixed its staged/untracked-file blind spot. The card's steal-this matches that fix, though it omits adding git status to the tools line, which the page says is needed. The product plug at the end doesn't gate the technique.

summary.title: themis: a customer support agent with code-enforced guardrails and an eval harness
summary.idea: Prompt-only rules let a support agent approve refunds it shouldn't, so this repo enforces limits in code at the tool-call layer and measures behaviour with a 45-scenario eval suite.
howItWorks: Support procedures live as markdown files in an aops folder, and the agent loads only the one it needs.
Every tool call passes through a guardrails module that checks identity verification and order ownership.
Refunds over $150 are routed to a human for approval rather than decided by the model.
A live trace shows the current procedure step, tool calls and each guardrail decision.
45 scenarios (normal, edge, attacks like prompt injection) are checked against backend state and graded by an LLM judge.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent ships, move one hard rule (like a spending limit) out of the prompt into a code check on the tool call, then run an eval that compares both versions.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building an agent that takes real actions, like refunds, and need evidence that code guardrails beat prompt instructions.
summary.quote: With the guardrails in code it was $0.

verdict.reason: The page backs the card: it moves rules like the $150 refund approval threshold, identity checks and order ownership out of the prompt into a code guardrail on every tool call, and a 45-scenario eval showed $2,541 in unapproved refunds with prompt-only rules versus $0 with code guardrails, though the README is brief on the mechanics.
